ab_frames.n: Existing reconstruction-based detection methods split the pipeline into two disconnected stages.
In the first stage, an input image is passed through a pre-trained diffusion model to produce a reconstructed image.
A conceptual barrier isolates the two stages, passing frozen representations forward without joint optimization.
The second stage computes the absolute reconstruction error and trains a backend classifier to predict whether the image is real or generated.
Crucially, this existing architecture lacks direct interaction between the diffusion model and the downstream classifier.
In contrast, the proposed framework unifies reconstruction and classification into an end-to-end training pipeline.
The Frequency Mask Refinement module filters out difficult-to-reconstruct mid-band frequencies to produce a pseudo-generated image.
Both the original and pseudo-generated images are passed to the diffusion autoencoder for parallel reconstruction.
Absolute difference operations calculate distinct reconstruction error maps for both the original and pseudo-generated inputs.
Absolute difference operations calculate distinct reconstruction error maps for both the original and pseudo-generated inputs.
These dual reconstruction error maps are concatenated and fed into the classifier to make the final real or generated prediction.
This integrated design ensures better alignment between artifact generation and artifact detection across the latent space.

ab_frames.n: The pipeline begins in the multi-resolution feature grid module.
A three-dimensional indoor scene containing various furniture objects is observed.
A virtual camera viewpoint casts rays toward the scene.
Along each viewing ray, points are sampled across space.
For an individual sample point labeled p, coordinates are queried.
Point p is mapped into a coarse three-dimensional feature grid.
Simultaneously, features are extracted from a finer-resolution grid.
The interpolated grid features are processed through a neural network.
The network outputs signed distance field values for each distinct object instance.
Taking the minimum across object values produces the overall scene signed distance field.
Next, the occlusion-aware object opacity module models visibility.
Individual object densities are derived along the ray.
The scene signed distance field yields the global scene transmittance curve.
The object densities are multiplied by the scene transmittance.
This produces occlusion-aware object opacity profiles along the ray.
An object opacity loss guides these opacity predictions.
Supervision is provided by two-dimensional instance masks for foreground objects.
Additional instance masks supervise the remaining objects in the scene.
Combining scene transmittance and scene density forms the volume rendering weight function.
Finally, the volume rendering module handles geometric regularization and multi-modal rendering.
An eikonal signed distance field loss regularizes spatial gradients.
A regularization loss penalizes signed distance discrepancies across objects.
A depth loss enforces consistency with geometric surface depths.
This directly optimizes the rendered scene depth map.
A normal loss supervises estimated surface orientations.
The loss supervises the rendered surface normal map.
Guidance cues are provided by a pretrained model encoder-decoder.
A reconstruction loss measures photometric differences.
This completes the rendering pipeline, reproducing the observed RGB scene image.

ab_frames.n: The pipeline begins with multi-view input images and corresponding object masks covering the scene with the bear statue.
These multi-view inputs construct the initial volume of Gaussians with the bear statue, denoted as G 1:N.
Depth is then rendered from this initial volume across all viewpoints to yield corresponding depth maps.
To infer the depth-guided inpainting mask, paired viewpoints with their respective images and masks are selected.
The object masks are applied to extract masked background images for each perspective.
Using rendered depth from the second view, background information is projected into view one.
This fusion isolates unobserved regions to produce a refined inpainting mask for the reference view.
Entering the inpainting-guided refinement stage, the refined mask guides inpainting to synthesize completed image and depth maps.
Through depth-guided projection, the inpainted depth is lifted into three-dimensional space as point cloud P1.
This geometry is then projected onto the other views to provide multi-view supervisory guidance.
Simultaneously, the reconstructed point cloud initializes the refined Gaussian volume representing the scene without the statue.
Rendering the reference view produces color and depth outputs that are supervised against the inpainted targets via the rendering loss.
Finally, rendering the other viewpoints and enforcing the cross loss ensures multi-view consistency across the entire scene.

ab_frames.n: The pipeline begins with parallel image and pressure sequences captured over time.
Each stream is processed through an Encoder followed by an LSAM block.
Outputs from both LSAM blocks are routed into the FCAM, the Fusion Cross-Attention Module, and then into the Regressor.
The Regressor outputs parameters theta and T, supervised by the pose loss and translation loss.
These parameters form the joint representation, supervised by three-D and contact losses, yielding three-D body pose reconstructions over time.
An Orthographic Projection is then applied to the joints, supervised by the two-D loss.
The internal architecture of the FCAM is detailed below, alongside an operations legend for matrix multiplication, addition, and concatenation.

The Image Feature branches into Image Value and Image Key, while the Pressure Feature becomes the Pressure Query. The Image Key and Pressure Query are combined via matrix multiplication and passed through SoftMax.
The SoftMax result undergoes matrix multiplication with the Image Value, is added to the Image Feature skip connection, and enters a Position-wise Feed-Forward block.
Finally, the output is concatenated with the Image Feature shortcut to produce the fused cross-attention output.

ab_frames.n: The pipeline begins at the Input stage.
The input includes a 3D point cloud representing the scene.
This is accompanied by RGB images along with depth images and camera poses.
In Step 1, 3D-Aware 2D Mask Tracking starts with superpoint selection from the point cloud.
Information from the superpoint, RGB images, and depth images is compiled into a histogram of projected points.
The histogram informs the pivot view selection.
The pivot view and superpoint then feed into SAM 2 Segmentation.
This produces a 2D mask in the pivot view.
The pivot mask, along with 3D cues, is directed into SAM 2 Tracking.
Tracking is performed via bidirectional 2D mask tracking, executing both a backward pass and a forward pass.
This process establishes the complete 2D mask track across frames.
Moving to Step 2, 3D Proposal Refinement Via Mask Optimization begins by lifting the 2D mask track to a 3D mask candidate.
The candidate is then refined via optimization using Algorithm 1.
This optimization outputs the final 3D proposal.
The proposals are combined into a class-agnostic 3D instance segmentation.
At the Output stage, this yields Open-Vocabulary 3D Instance Segmentation and Open-Ended 3D Instance Segmentation.
Using CLIP and LLM modules, instances receive labels such as table, TV, desktop, and monitor.

ab_frames.n: The initialization process begins with the frozen, pre-trained 3-D Gaussian Splatting model.
The model undergoes Frequency Guided Densification, labeled FGD.
The densification workflow is detailed below across two operational phases.
In Phase one, the initial 3-D Gaussians are evaluated based on their individual contribution to rendering quality.
The contribution scale defines the degree of visual impact each Gaussian provides.
Gaussians with low rendering contribution are removed from the representation.
Phase two begins by rendering multi-view images from the remaining Gaussians.
Each rendered view is partitioned into a uniform grid of image patches.
A Discrete Fourier Transform is computed for every patch.
This converts each spatial patch into a corresponding frequency domain patch.
In the high-frequency detection stage, the transformed patch spectrum is extracted.
The transformed patch is multiplied element-wise by a quadratic mask.
Regions identified with high-frequency content are highlighted and selected.
The 3-D Gaussians located within these high-frequency areas are split into finer primitives.
Densification concludes, yielding the modified, frozen 3-D Gaussian model.
A gradient mask is constructed over the Gaussian position, color, opacity, rotation, and scale parameters.
In the fine-tuning process, the parameters of the target 3-D Gaussian model are unfrozen.
The model renders a 2-D viewpoint image.
A Discrete Wavelet Transform is applied directly to the rendered image.
The transformation isolates the low-frequency component.
This low-frequency representation feeds into a pre-trained, frozen decoder.
The decoder produces the decoded message output.
Simultaneously, the high-frequency components from the wavelet transform are routed down.
A ground truth image provides the visual reference.
The ground truth is likewise processed with a Discrete Wavelet Transform.
This extracts the ground truth high-frequency sub-bands.
Reconstruction loss and perceptual loss are evaluated between the rendered and ground truth images.
A wavelet loss compares the high frequencies of the rendered and ground truth views.
A fixed target message acts as the supervision signal for message decoding.
A message loss computes the error between the decoded message and the fixed message.
All reconstruction, wavelet, and message loss terms are summed into the total loss.
The total loss flows into the optimizer.
The optimizer updates are masked through a Hadamard product before adjusting the fine-tuned 3-D Gaussians.

ab_frames.n: The workflow begins on the left with Data Preparation.
A Reference Frame undergoes Object Replacement to isolate the target object.
From the Input Frame, Box Detection identifies hand and object bounding boxes, while Hand Mesh Augmentation generates hand mesh representations.
The processed components then feed into the Training Pipeline.
A Reference Image of the target object is passed to a frozen VAE Encoder.
The encoded features enter the Reference U-Net, which contains multiple Self Attention blocks.
In parallel, Hand Mesh sequences are processed through ControlNet.
Layout Guidance bounding boxes are passed into the Layout Encoder.
The encoded layout features are combined with Noise.
The noisy input enters the Denoising U-Net, which alternates between Self Attention, Hand Attention, Object Attention, and Temp Attention layers, conditioned by the Reference U-Net and ControlNet.
The output of the Denoising U-Net is routed through a frozen VAE Decoder to produce the final Generated Frames.
At the bottom, the HOI Restoration Module expands the Hand Attention and Object Attention mechanisms.
In Hand Attention, key and value pairs from a Hand Texture Memory Bank combine with a query via Cross Attention, pass through a residual addition, and are modulated by a Hand Mask.
Likewise, Object Attention takes keys and values from an Object Texture Memory Bank into Cross Attention, adds a residual query, and multiplies by an Object Mask.

description: Crops a rectangular region from an image, as a PNG file or an embeddable data URI.

# Region Crop

Crops a rectangular region from an image.

```
python scripts/crop_region.py <image> <x> <y> <width> <height> --out <file.png> [--data-uri]
```

- **Input:** an image and a box in pixel coordinates.
- **Output:** a PNG file; with `--data-uri`, also prints a `data:image/png;base64,...` string.
- **Requires:** `pip install pillow`.
region-crop.script:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Crop a rectangular region (pixel coordinates) from an image."""
import argparse
import base64
import io
import sys

from PIL import Image


def main() -> None:
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    p.add_argument("image")
    p.add_argument("x", type=float)
    p.add_argument("y", type=float)
    p.add_argument("width", type=float)
    p.add_argument("height", type=float)
    p.add_argument("--out", required=True, help="output PNG path")
    p.add_argument("--data-uri", action="store_true",
                   help="also print the crop as a data:image/png;base64 URI")
    a = p.parse_args()

    img = Image.open(a.image).convert("RGBA")
    W, H = img.size
    left = max(0, round(a.x))
    top = max(0, round(a.y))
    right = min(W, round(a.x + a.width))
    bottom = min(H, round(a.y + a.height))
    if right <= left or bottom <= top:
        sys.exit(f"empty crop: box outside image of size {W}x{H}")

    crop = img.crop((left, top, right, bottom))
    crop.save(a.out, "PNG")
    print(f"saved {a.out} ({right - left}x{bottom - top} at {left},{top}; image {W}x{H})")
    if a.data_uri:
        buf = io.BytesIO()
        crop.save(buf, "PNG")
        print("data:image/png;base64," + base64.b64encode(buf.getvalue()).decode())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# Render Frames

Renders an SVG file to PNG images in a headless browser.

```
python scripts/render_frames.py <file.svg> --out <dir> [--times 0,1.5,3 | --every <seconds> --until <seconds>]
```

- **Input:** an SVG file and the times to render (default: time 0).
- **Output:** one PNG per requested time, in `<dir>`.
- **Requires:** `pip install playwright`, then `python -m playwright install chromium`.
render-frames.script:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Render an SVG file (static or animated) to PNG images at chosen times.

Uses headless Chromium via Playwright. CSS animations and SMIL animations are
both paused and seeked to each requested time before the screenshot.
Requires: pip install playwright && python -m playwright install chromium
"""
import argparse
import pathlib
import re

from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright


def svg_size(svg_text: str) -> tuple[int, int]:
    vb = re.search(r'viewBox\s*=\s*"([^"]+)"', svg_text)
    if vb:
        parts = [float(v) for v in re.split(r"[\s,]+", vb.group(1).strip())]
        if len(parts) == 4:
            return max(1, round(parts[2])), max(1, round(parts[3]))
    w = re.search(r'<svg[^>]*\swidth\s*=\s*"([\d.]+)', svg_text)
    h = re.search(r'<svg[^>]*\sheight\s*=\s*"([\d.]+)', svg_text)
    if w and h:
        return round(float(w.group(1))), round(float(h.group(1)))
    return 1280, 720


SEEK_JS = """
(t) => {
  for (const s of document.querySelectorAll('svg')) {
    if (s.pauseAnimations) { s.pauseAnimations(); s.setCurrentTime(t); }
  }
  for (const a of document.getAnimations()) { a.pause(); a.currentTime = t * 1000; }
}
"""


def main() -> None:
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    p.add_argument("svg")
    p.add_argument("--out", required=True, help="output directory")
    p.add_argument("--times", help="comma-separated times in seconds, e.g. 0,1.5,3")
    p.add_argument("--every", type=float, help="render every N seconds ...")
    p.add_argument("--until", type=float, help="... up to this time in seconds")
    a = p.parse_args()

    if a.times:
        times = [float(t) for t in a.times.split(",") if t.strip()]
    elif a.every and a.until is not None:
        n = int(a.until / a.every + 1e-9)
        times = [round(i * a.every, 3) for i in range(n + 1)]
    else:
        times = [0.0]

    svg_path = pathlib.Path(a.svg).resolve()
    text = svg_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    w, h = svg_size(text)
    out = pathlib.Path(a.out)
    out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    html = ("<!DOCTYPE html><html><head><style>html,body{margin:0;padding:0;background:#fff}"
            "svg{display:block;width:%dpx;height:%dpx}</style></head><body>%s</body></html>"
            % (w, h, text))

    with sync_playwright() as pw:
        browser = pw.chromium.launch()
        page = browser.new_page(viewport={"width": w, "height": h})
        page.set_content(html, wait_until="load")
        for t in times:
            page.evaluate(SEEK_JS, t)
            page.wait_for_timeout(50)
            f = out / f"frame_t{t:07.3f}.png"
            page.screenshot(path=str(f), clip={"x": 0, "y": 0, "width": w, "height": h})
            print(f)
        browser.close()
